messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 24
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Pharmacist
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 58

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Moral Violation: People misbehaving, Funerals/Graves: Funerals, cemeteries, or grief-related events, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Threat: Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think, False Alarms: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
  Memory: No Coherent Story: I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself, Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt, Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable., Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma, Lost Meaning: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

At 24, Matiu had been working as a pharmacist for just over a year when his older cousin, who had helped raise him in their Samoan American family, was killed after a night of heavy drinking. The account Matiu gives of that night never comes in a clean line. He can say there was a call, that people were shouting, that he ended up at the hospital and later at the funeral, but when he tries to put the hours together he loses the sequence and goes blank. Some parts return with a crushing stab of guilt—especially the thought that, as the one in the family with medical training, he should somehow have prevented what happened or understood sooner how serious it was. At other times he describes the same night in a flat, detached way that disturbs him, as if he is reciting something that happened to somebody else.

In the months afterward, what settled in most deeply was not only grief but a conviction that his life had been ruined. He had come to believe that the person he had been before—easygoing, social, proud of finally becoming a pharmacist—was gone for good. Nothing felt meaningful in the way it once had; even work, which had been a source of purpose, now seemed hollow. That sense that happiness had been lost fed directly into how on edge he felt in his own body. He began living as if some further blow was always about to land, shoulders tight, jaw set, pulse jumping before he had even worked out what had caught his attention. When his body surged into alarm in ordinary moments, he took it as further proof that the trauma had permanently damaged him, that his life really had been destroyed rather than shaken.

His view of himself and his future also shaped the way he related to the memory. Because he was certain he had failed someone he loved and that nothing worthwhile remained ahead of him, remembering the event pulled him quickly toward guilt. The more he told himself that this death had stripped life of meaning, the less he could hold the memory together as a full account; instead it broke into jagged fragments or turned strangely numb. He does not remember and then conclude that life is over so much as approach the memory already convinced it confirms that conclusion.

Those same beliefs have made the world feel full of loaded reminders. Since he sees the trauma as the point at which happiness and meaning ended, he scans for anything that belongs to that world of loss. Funerals are unbearable; when a patient at the pharmacy mentions an upcoming burial, he feels a jolt of dread before he can think. Cemeteries and grief rituals feel contaminated, not simply sad. The smell of alcohol is especially potent. At work, opening the counseling window for a customer whose breath carries liquor can make his stomach drop and his chest tighten instantly. He has also become sharply reactive to people behaving badly in public—customers arguing, someone being loud and careless in the parking lot—because it fits with the way he now sees the world: reckless behavior destroys lives, and one moment of it can take everything.

Once a trigger catches him, memory follows in the form it usually does now: incomplete, guilty, and disjointed. The alcohol smell at the pharmacy can bring back the hospital corridor without a clear beginning or end, just flashes and the certainty that he should have done more. A funeral announcement can leave him with an image of standing beside his family, emotionally blunted and ashamed of that blunting, unable to tell himself a whole story about what he was seeing or feeling. His reactions also run in the other direction. Because the memory is so fractured and saturated with guilt, he is left vulnerable to whatever resembles one piece of it; the gaps seem to make the reminders spread. Not being able to organize what happened means that funerals, graveyards, and even the sour smell of alcohol continue to stand in for the whole event, and the guilty fragments make other people’s misbehavior feel intolerably charged.

Over time this has narrowed his life. In the pharmacy he keeps his interactions brisk and avoids lingering near customers who smell of alcohol. He has stopped attending family graveside visits, which has been noticed and quietly resented by relatives who see absence where he experiences sheer overwhelm. What frightened him most by the time he sought help was how automatic everything had become: his body launching into alarm before thought, ordinary scenes turning into reminders, reminders collapsing him into guilt, and each episode seeming to confirm that he was no longer the person he had been. He came in after realizing he was starting to dread going to work and had begun to think that if this continued, there would be nothing in his life left that still felt like his own.
